Teachable Machine builds the model. Scratch uses its predictions to make something happen.

A new image project

  1. Open Teachable Machine and select Get Started.
  2. Choose Image Project.
  3. Choose Standard Image Model.
Open Teachable Machine ↗

Classes are the categories to recognize

  1. Click the pencil beside each class name.
  2. Name your classes Hello, Nick! and Let’s Go, Knicks!.
  3. Choose a clearly different gesture for each class.

The class name is a label. The model learns visual patterns, not the meaning of “Knicks.”

Training examples

  1. Select Webcam and allow camera access.
  2. Make the first gesture and use Hold to Record.
  3. Repeat for the second class. Aim for about 50–100 images per class as a classroom starting point.

Add variation.
Change position, distance and angle while keeping the gesture recognizable.

Keep classes balanced.
Use similar numbers of images. Avoid using a different background for each gesture.

Many nearly identical frames provide less variety than examples collected in different conditions.

Training the model

  1. Keep the default settings for your first attempt.
  2. Click Train Model and leave the tab open.
  3. After training, use Preview to try your gestures.

Training adjusts the model so its predictions better match the class labels in your examples.

Under Advanced, you can find epochs, batch size and learning rate. Let’s unpack them.

Epochs: how many practice rounds?

Your model practices using the images you collected.

Epochs tells it how many rounds to practice.

1 epoch = 1 practice round

One round uses all the training images.

10 epochs means 10 rounds with the same training images. It does not mean collecting 10 new images.

Batch size: how many images in a group?

During each practice round, the model looks at images in groups.

After each group, it adjusts to reduce its mistakes.

Batch size 16 = 16 images per group

Look at a group of images. Make an adjustment. Continue with the next group.

Batch size controls the group size during training. Keep the default for today.

Learning rate: how big is each adjustment?

During training, the model adjusts to reduce its mistakes.

Learning rate controls how big each adjustment is.

Too small

Tiny adjustments can make learning slow.

Too large

Big adjustments can make learning unstable.

Why do we care? A suitable learning rate helps the model improve steadily. Keep the default for today.

The settings to use today

Keep the default settings for your first model.

SettingEasy way to remember
EpochsNumber of practice rounds
Batch sizeImages in each group
Learning rateSize of each adjustment

First, train and test your model. If it makes mistakes, look for better or more varied training examples.

Testing with new examples

  1. Try each gesture in the Preview window.
  2. Move closer, farther away or slightly to the side.
  3. Try a different person or different lighting.
  4. Record when the prediction matches your intended class.

Use examples you did not collect for training. Success on familiar images alone does not show that the model generalizes.

Confidence and accuracy

Confidence

How strongly the model favors a class for one image.

Hello, Nick! — 96%

Accuracy

How often the model is correct across many test images.

90 correct out of 100 = 90% accuracy

A model can have high confidence and still be wrong. A 96% confidence score does not guarantee that prediction is correct.

Finding errors

Try to fool your model

Try an unclear gesture. Show neither gesture. Ask a classmate to try.

With only two classes, the model still assigns scores to those two options.

Improve the examples

Add examples of the situations it misses. Consider a third Neutral / No gesture class for your own project.

Retrain, then repeat the same tests.

Ask: Is the model learning the gesture, or using a shortcut such as the background or person?

Exporting your model

  1. Click Export Model.
  2. Choose TensorFlow.js, then Upload my model.
  3. Copy the shareable model URL and keep it for Scratch.
Try Nick’s example ↗
https://teachablemachine.withgoogle.com/models/w_DQ4_ljC/

The model URL loads the trained model. Save your editable Teachable Machine project separately if you want to change its training data later.

Nick’s example is not perfect! Try it, notice its mistakes, and think about how we could improve it.

Scratch with TM2Scratch

  1. Open Stretch3 in Chrome.
  2. Click Add Extension at the bottom left.
  3. Choose TM2Scratch.
  4. Drag the image classification model URL block into the code area.
Open Stretch3 ↗

Stretch3 is a Scratch-based editor with additional extensions. TM2Scratch connects your image model to the blocks.

The big picture: your model + Scratch

The camera provides an image. The model predicts a label. Scratch runs the matching script.

① Model URL
The green block at the top connects Scratch to your trained model.

② Knicks script
The upper script responds to “Let’s Go, Knicks!”

③ Hello script
The lower script responds to “Hello, Nick!”

Adding your own voice recordings

  1. Select your sprite and open the Sounds tab.
  2. Open the Choose a Sound menu at the bottom left. Select Record.
  3. Click the record button, say “Let’s Go, Knicks!”, stop, and click Save.
  4. Name the sound Let’s Go, Knicks!. Repeat to record Hello, Nick!.
  5. Return to Code. Select each recording in the matching play sound […] until done block.

You can also choose Upload Sound to use an existing audio recording.

The Knicks script: top to bottom

  1. image classification model URLPaste your model URL. Click this block once to load your model.
  2. when received image label: Let’s Go, Knicks!When the model recognizes this label, check the script below.
  3. if speaking = 0 thenContinue only when the switch equals 0.
  4. set speaking to 1Change the switch to 1 before playing the sound.
  5. play sound Let’s Go, Knicks! until donePlay your Knicks recording and wait for it to finish.
  6. say Let’s Go, Knicks! for 2 secondsShow the message in the sprite’s speech bubble.

The Hello script: top to bottom

  1. when received image label: Hello, Nick!When the model recognizes this label, check the script below.
  2. if speaking = 1 thenContinue only when the switch equals 1.
  3. set speaking to 0Change the switch back to 0 before playing the sound.
  4. play sound Hello, Nick! until donePlay your Hello recording and wait for it to finish.
  5. say Hello, Nick! for 2 secondsShow the Hello message in the sprite’s speech bubble.

Why use a variable?

The camera keeps sending predictions. The same label can arrive again and again.

Without the condition

Every repeated label can trigger its sound again. The application can become noisy!

With the variable + condition

speaking remembers which response is allowed next. After Knicks plays, it must wait for Hello before playing again.

Switch valueAllowed nextAfter the response
0KnicksSwitch becomes 1
1HelloSwitch becomes 0

Setup: Variables → Make a Variable → name it speaking. Click set speaking to 0 once to begin.

The variable works together with the if condition. This example alternates responses. Rapid label changes may still trigger sounds close together.
